catalog_quote: An interesting dialect difference is thet in Takum it is the end of a rising tone that is stressed, while in Wukari it is the beginning that is stressed. Thus forms nays the two dialects whionh-are identical in tone are quite different in stress. The phonemic status of stress, here and elsewhere, has not been completely investigated. However, there is no evidence that it is phonemic, and in at least some phrases there appears to be some freedom in the position of stress, ... [sec. 1.9] The two dialects have the same tonemes, although the distribution of these tonemes in relation to morphemes is quite different in the two. ... Note in particular the following twelve sentences, each of which is perfectly natural and sensible, and each of which differs from all the others only in tone, in either dialect

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every fragment of the deciding quotation is present verbatim in the held scanned of Welmers 1968 at sec. 1.9.4 (lines 1145-1158) and sec. 1.9 (lines 907, 1015-1017); locator is correct apart from the scanned page marker reading '_ 2h -' for '- 24 -'. (2) Deciding source: a 1968 descriptive grammar sketch (163 pp) by Welmers, with a phonology chapter, explicit three-level toneme analysis with twelve-way tonal minimal sentences, and an explicit statement that stress shows no evidence of being phonemic and varies in position. Glottolog's bibliography for juku1254 contains no phonology/tone/stress study; its only 'grammar' (Shimizu 1980) is shown by the Google Books record to be a grammar of the Wukari (Wapan) language, so it does not supersede Welmers for Takum.
